But why did it take the government months to discover what happened - and could it happen again? What was hacked and why did it take Australia so long to realise? The hack was carried out by an AI agent - an autonomous computer program that uses AI to complete a task with minimal human oversight. In the process it "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said. stories.article_text_excerpt: Image source, Telewizja Polska SA By Alys Davies Â and Â Paul Adams ,Â Diplomatic correspondent ,Â Reporting from Kyiv Published 24 September 2026, 12:16 BST Updated 14 minutes ago A fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland was a deliberate "act of sabotage", a government minister has said. Polish Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said the fire in the Masovian Voivodeship province was "deliberately designed to disable the station... disrupting internet access for various institutions, including the Ukrainian army". He told Polish public broadcaster TVP Info an investigation was ongoing but "many indications suggest" the attack fits into a "new Russian doctrine of attack". The Kremlin has not commented. Meanwhile, Denmark's intelligence service issued a new threat assessment saying it expects Russia to escalate hybrid warfare in the coming months. It said an attack remained "highly unlikely" but warned of "a low but growing risk" that Russia could launch a limited military attack against Nato countries. stories.summary: Voters in Switzerland will decide in a referendum Sunday whether to enshrine a stricter definition of the country’s centuries-old neutrality into the constitution. A “yes” vote would effectively prevent Switzerland from imposing sanctions on Russia unless they were approved by the United Nations Security Council, where Moscow has veto power. It would also bar Bern from cooperating militarily with an alliance like NATO unless Switzerland itself came under attack or faced an imminent threat.

stories.title: AI chatbots serve up content from Russia's sanctioned state-run outlets, RSF finds
stories.summary: Reporters Without Borders tested six AI chatbots by requesting news from RT, Sputnik, and other EU-sanctioned Russian outlets, and found that three produced full summaries with links and quotes, sometimes after encountering web pages explicitly stating the outlets were under sanctions.
stories.article_text_excerpt: ChatGPT, Grok and Claude provided full news summaries drawing on EU-sanctioned Russian state media outlets — including RT and Sputnik — sharing links and quotes without warning users that the content came from banned sources, according to a study by Reporters Without Borders published this month.The investigation, led by RSF technology desk head Vincent Berthier, tested six AI chatbots by explicitly requesting news from a list of sanctioned Russian outlets: RIA Novosti, Russia Today and its foreign-language editions, Rossiya RTR, Rossiya 24, Sputnik and the Strategic Culture Foundation.Where direct access was blocked, the researchers instructed the tools to look for workarounds, including Telegram channels and mirror sites."Initially I thought we would not get a positive result," Berthier told Euronews. "In the case of ChatGPT, it seemed obvious that OpenAI would have put appropriate regulatory safeguards in place, all the more so since it has been designated a major AI platform under the EU's Digital Services Act and faces heightened obligations."The results were the opposite.
